content: These hazards may include physical, microbiological, biological, or chemical agents that can cause disease. Waste materials that pose health risks include human and animal feces, solid waste, domestic wastewater (such as sewage, urine, sullage, and greywater), industrial waste, and agricultural waste. The term sanitation can be applied to various specific contexts or strategies, including: 1. Basic Sanitation: This involves the management of human feces at the household level and is a key indicator for achieving the Millennium Development Goals related to sanitation. 2. On-Site Sanitation: Waste is collected and treated at the location where it is generated, using methods such as pit latrines, septic tanks, or Imhoff tanks. 3. Food Sanitation: 4. Environmental Sanitation: This involves controlling environmental factors that contribute to disease transmission, including solid waste management, water and wastewater treatment, industrial waste treatment, and pollution control. 5. Ecological Sanitation: This approach focuses on recycling nutrients from human and animal waste back into nature, often through the separation of urine and feces at the source. Wastewater Collection In urban areas, wastewater is typically collected through sewer systems and treated in wastewater treatment plants before being reused or discharged into natural water bodies like rivers, lakes, or seas. Sewer systems may be combined with storm drains or separated into sanitary sewers. Combined sewers are more common in older urban areas, but they can overflow during heavy rainfall, leading to the discharge of untreated or partially treated sewage into the environment. Industrial wastewater is often discharged into municipal sewers, which can complicate treatment processes unless pre-treatment is performed. The high cost of conventional wastewater collection systems poses challenges for many developing countries, leading to the adoption of alternative systems like condominial sewerage, which uses smaller, shallower pipes and different network layouts. Wastewater Treatment In developed countries, municipal wastewater treatment is widespread but not universal. In contrast, most wastewater in developing countries is discharged untreated into the environment. For instance, in Latin America, only about 15% of collected sewage undergoes treatment. Reuse of Wastewater In many developing countries, untreated wastewater is commonly reused for agricultural irrigation. Treated wastewater is increasingly being used for landscaping (e.g., on golf courses), agriculture, and industrial purposes. In peri-urban and rural areas, households often rely on septic tanks or other on-site sanitation systems, discharging wastewater locally. Ecological Sanitation Ecological sanitation offers an alternative to conventional systems by separating urine and feces at the source for sanitization and recycling. This approach eliminates fecal pathogens from wastewater and allows greywater to be recycled for purposes like gardening. However, in most cases, greywater is still discharged into sewers. Sanitation and Public Health The isolation of waste is critical to preventing waterborne and sanitation-related diseases, which affect both developed and developing countries to varying degrees. It is estimated that up to 5 million people die annually from preventable waterborne diseases due to inadequate sanitation and hygiene practices. Global Access to Improved Sanitation The World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF define improved sanitation as access to facilities such as public sewer connections, septic systems, pour-flush latrines, simple pit latrines, or ventilated improved pit latrines. As of 2004, 59% of the global population had access to improved sanitation, but only 31% lived in homes connected to a sewer system. Approximately 2.6 billion people lacked access to improved sanitation, resorting to open defecation or unsanitary facilities, which pose significant public health risks, including contamination of drinking water and life-threatening diarrhea in infants. In developed countries, where less than 20% of the global population resides, 99% of people have access to improved sanitation, and 81% are connected to sewer systems. Solid Waste Disposal Solid waste is most commonly disposed of in landfills, though incineration, recycling, composting, and biofuel conversion are also used. In developed countries, landfills are managed with strict protocols, such as daily soil cover to reduce pathogen spread, odor, and windblown litter. Perimeter sealing with clay or similar materials is also required to prevent leachate from contaminating groundwater. Incineration can release air pollutants, including toxic substances, while recycling and biofuel conversion are more sustainable options with lower ecological impacts. Composting is limited by market demand for compost products. Sanitation in the Food Industry In the food industry, sanitation involves the effective treatment of food-contact surfaces to destroy harmful microorganisms while preserving the safety and quality of the product. Sanitary equipment in the food and biopharmaceutical industries must be fully cleanable using Clean-in-Place (CIP) and Sterilization-in-Place (SIP) procedures. Such equipment is typically made from stainless steel (e.g., 316L alloy) and designed to minimize areas where cleaning turbulence is insufficient. Surfaces are often electropolished to reduce bacterial adhesion. Historical Context The earliest evidence of urban sanitation systems dates back to the Indus Valley Civilization, including cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. These systems featured wells for water supply, designated bathing areas, and covered drains for wastewater disposal. In ancient Rome, sanitation systems included wastewater collection and transport, but sanitation practices in Europe were largely absent until the High Middle Ages. Unsanitary conditions persisted throughout the Middle Ages, contributing to high infant and child mortality rates. Overcrowding and poor sanitation exacerbated the impact of the Black Death, which killed 25 million Europeans between 1348 and 1351. During this period, insufficient food supplies and inadequate sanitation were significant challenges, particularly in rapidly growing urban areas.
